lead: Ice on an aircraft destroys lift, adds weight and blinds the sensors that tell the crew their speed and height. Ice protection keeps the critical surfaces clear: hot air or electric heaters stop ice forming; rubber boots and fluid break it off after it has formed. Rain protection keeps the windscreen clear so the runway stays visible.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for the bleed air that feeds thermal anti-icing.

blocks.text: Clouds between 0 °C and about −20 °C carry supercooled droplets: water still liquid below freezing. A droplet freezes the moment it touches a surface at or below 0 °C. Wing leading edges, spinners, windscreens and probes are exactly that in flight, so ice builds within minutes.

items: Extra weight: a 3 mm layer over 12 m² of wing is 32.4 kg on one side, before any lift is lost.
Loss of lift: the rough, lumpy leading edge breaks smooth airflow, so the maximum lift coefficient Cₗₘₐₓ falls and drag rises.
Earlier stall: lower Cₗₘₐₓ and higher weight both push the stall speed up.
Tailplane trouble: the horizontal tail has a thinner section, so a thin ice layer there can take away pitch control just when the crew flares.
Blind sensors: ice in a pitot head gives false airspeed; ice on a static port gives false altitude as well. Unit 3 covers these instruments.
Engine and propeller: shed ice damages compressor blades or stalls the engine; ice on a propeller causes vibration and loss of thrust.

blocks.where: V<sub>stall</sub> is the stall speed in m/s; W is the aircraft weight in N, including the ice; ρ is air density in kg/m³; S is wing area in m²; C<sub>Lmax</sub> is the maximum lift coefficient, which falls when the leading edge is rough.

blocks.text: Ice also costs time: after freezing rain the aircraft needs fluid sprayed by a de-icing rig before departure, and the crew checks the fluid's holdover time.

Two words carry most of the marks. Anti-icing prevents ice forming on a surface: the skin is held above 0 °C, or coated with fluid that stops the droplet freezing. De-icing lets ice form and then removes it. One aircraft often uses both: hot air on the wing leading edges and a boot on the tail, or boots on the wing and electric heat on the probes.

Wing and tail leading edges, engine inlet lips on transports
Heater mats bonded under the skin, switched in cycles
Pitot heads, drain masts, windscreens, propellers
Glycol seeps through a porous leading edge and lowers the freezing point of the water landing on it
Small aircraft and some business jets; limited by fluid carried
Rubber tubes inflate, the skin stretches, brittle ice cracks off; de-icing only
A coil under the skin drives it out in a fast pulse and shatters the ice

blocks.text: Bleed air is not free. It comes from the engine compressor, so thrust falls and fuel burn rises while anti-icing is on, and the ducting, valves and regulators add weight and maintenance. Electric mats need generator capacity instead, so they suit small areas and short duty cycles.

Pneumatic boots need care. Cycled while the ice is only a fraction of a millimetre thick, the boot cannot crack it cleanly; the thin film stays and later ice bridges across the inflated shape. Boots are cycled only after a few millimetres have built up, with a timer doing it while the aircraft is in icing cloud.

sections.h3: Protected areas, ice detection and rain removal

blocks.text: Protection is fitted where ice does the most harm, not over the whole airframe; weight and cost forbid that.

items: Wing leading edges from root to tip, and the leading edges of the horizontal and vertical tail.
Engine inlet lips, the spinner, and on some types the first compressor stage.
Propeller blades, heated by electric mats at the root.
Pitot heads, static ports and the air temperature probe, all electrically heated, because no flight is safe on false air data.
Windscreen, heated electrically or by hot air, for both ice and mist.
Drain masts and drain lines, so the drains do not block or tear off.

blocks.text: Detection can be visual from the cockpit, which is why the ice inspection light sits on the fuselage side. Automatic detectors use a probe in the airstream: a vibrating rod whose frequency changes as ice mass builds, or an optical or conductivity sensor. The signal lights an annunciator, tells the crew when to select anti-icing, and on some aircraft starts the boot cycle. Unit 4 shows how such a discrete signal reaches the display.

Rain removal works on the windscreen alone. Wipers use an electric motor and linkage, and air pressure holds the blade on the glass. Rain repellent is a hydrophobic coating applied on the ground, or a fluid sprayed on, that makes water bead and blow away. Hot air or electric heat raises the glass temperature so rain evaporates and mist clears. Some fast aircraft carry no wiper at all and rely on heat and repellent, because the arm is a hazard at high speed.

examples.question: A 3 mm thick layer of clear ice forms over 12 m² of wing leading edge on one side. Take the density of ice as 900 kg/m³. (a) Find the volume in m³. (b) Find the mass in kg. (c) State one effect of this mass.
steps: That is one wing only, before the other wing and the tail; the extra weight raises stall speed through V_stall = √(2W ÷ (ρ S C_Lmax)).
examples.answer: The ice has a volume of 0.036 m³ and a mass of 32.4 kg on that one wing.

thickness_mm = 3
area_m2 = 12
density = 900
thickness_m = thickness_mm / 1000
volume = thickness_m * area_m2
mass = volume * density

examples.question: A 2 mm ice layer forms over 9 m² of horizontal tailplane. Ice density is 900 kg/m³. Find the volume and the mass.
steps: Small mass, but on a thin tail section it is enough to change the pitching moment, which is why the tail is protected.
examples.answer: The tailplane carries 0.018 m³ of ice, a mass of 16.2 kg.

traps: Calling a pneumatic boot anti-icing. It is de-icing: it lets ice form and then cracks it off.
Listing only the wing when asked where protection is fitted. Tailplane, engine inlet, propeller, pitot and static heads, windscreen and drain masts all count.
Cycling the boots as soon as the first ice appears. A very thin layer does not crack cleanly and later ice bridges over it.
Unit slip in the ice-mass sum: 3 mm is 0.003 m, not 0.03 m. A factor of ten gives 324 kg instead of 32.4 kg.
Forgetting that bleed-air anti-icing steals compressor air, so thrust falls and fuel burn rises while the system is on.

quiz.a: Anti-icing prevents ice forming, for example by keeping the skin above 0 °C with hot air. De-icing removes ice after it has formed, for example by inflating a rubber boot so the ice cracks off.

quiz.q: Name four areas of an aircraft, other than the wing, that need ice protection.
quiz.a: Any four of: horizontal and vertical tail leading edges, engine inlet lip, propeller blades, pitot head and static port, windscreen, drain masts, air temperature probe.

quiz.q: Why does a rough, iced leading edge raise the stall speed?
quiz.a: Roughness makes the airflow separate earlier, so the maximum lift coefficient C_Lmax falls. In V_stall = √(2W ÷ (ρ S C_Lmax)) a smaller C_Lmax raises the stall speed. The added ice weight raises W, which raises it further.

quiz.q: Why is a thin ice layer on the horizontal tail more dangerous than the same layer on the wing?
quiz.a: The tail section is thinner with a shorter chord, so a given ice thickness is a much larger fraction of the chord. The tail also works at small angles of attack in cruise, where roughness hurts, and the crew needs tail lift in the flare. Losing it gives a pitch-down at low height.

quiz.q: A 2 mm ice layer forms over 9 m² of tailplane. Ice density is 900 kg/m³. Find the volume and the mass.
A crew selects the pneumatic boots the moment the first ice appears. Later they find ice still building on the boots. Explain what is happening and what they should do.
quiz.a: This is ice bridging. The first layer is too thin to crack off when the boot inflates; the boot deflates, the film stays, and later ice bridges across the inflated shape so the boot can no longer break it. The crew should wait until about 5 mm has built up before the first cycle, then let the timer cycle the boots while in icing cloud.

quiz.q: Compare bleed-air thermal anti-icing with electro-thermal mats for a twin turboprop on a regional route.
quiz.a: Bleed air protects a large area continuously but takes compressor air, so thrust and fuel burn suffer, and it needs ducts, valves and regulators along the leading edge. Electric mats need no ducting and route easily along a small surface, but they load the generators. A common split on such an aircraft is boots on the wing for de-icing, with electric heat on the propellers, probes and windscreen.

quiz.q: Why is a wiper not the only rain removal method on a fast aircraft?
quiz.a: At high speed the airflow and the wiper arm load the blade, and it can lift off the glass or be damaged. Heat and rain repellent keep the windscreen clear without a moving arm, so some aircraft rely on those alone.

beyond: Not for the exam. Bleedless designs heat the leading edge electrically, trading compressor air for generator power. Research follows icephobic coatings that stop droplets sticking at all, and electro-expulsive or hybrid systems that shatter ice with a short pulse instead of steady heat. Optical and ultrasonic detectors feed the flight computer directly instead of a panel lamp. Search for 'electro-expulsive de-icing' and 'icephobic coating' to go further.
